startup.name: Klaimee
startup.description: Insurance, certification and risk evaluation for companies that deploy AI agents, covering losses that cyber and E&O policies exclude. Self serve. Two founders: a former SafetyWing general manager who grew an insurance product from 5M to 60M revenue, and an AI engineer. Batch Spring 2026.

yc_acceptance.basis: Test note: the company was accepted, so this is an if accepted view. A blind prior starts near 1 percent, and the factors in the YC acceptance table are applied loosely here. Not part of the scored test.
yc_acceptance.why_it_fails: YC might decline because insurance needs licenses, capacity from reinsurers and loss data a two person team does not have, and Armilla (YC W22) already sells AI liability cover. Interviewers may doubt a self serve product can price risk no one has loss history on.

anchors.source: Ran python3 -I scripts/base_rates.py --industry Fintech --years 2022-2025 --calibration-only (only 26 companies, anecdote): seed 50 / 57 / 62, series A cond 23 percent (n=13), series B cond 0 (n=3). Also B2B 2022-2025: seed known 59, A cond 26 percent, B cond 16 percent.
anchors.adjustment_reason: Slightly below the 57 percent Fintech anchor (anecdotal, n=23) because insurance startups need partners before raising; offset by an operator with proven insurance growth and an AI hot topic. The seed step here means a round above the standard 500K YC deal within about 12 months, and the anchor is for any seed ever, so the 12 month window pulls it down while a hot category pushes it up.

bands.rationale: Small round just above the YC check, mostly angels, if traction is thin.

ladder.why_it_fails: A round above the YC check fails if the company cannot show a carrier or MGA partner willing to put paper behind the policy, or a single paying insured. Investors in insurtech expect licensed capacity. Analogs like armilla-ai raised only a seed and obie and shepherd took years to build.

ladder.why_it_fails: Series A fails if premiums stay small, losses are unpredictable or the carrier partner pulls capacity. With no loss history, investors worry about adverse selection and regulatory approvals can take a year or more, as insurance startups have shown. Insurtech analogs such as armilla-ai, shepherd and obie show that licensing, capacity and loss experience, not the pitch, set the pace of each step.

Leader round with a larger raise as the company becomes a category name.

ladder.why_it_fails: Series C fails if the AI risk market does not grow into large premiums or if a big carrier or Lloyd's syndicate owns the line. Capital requirements are high for a young insurer. Insurtech analogs such as armilla-ai, shepherd and obie show that licensing, capacity and loss experience, not the pitch, set the pace of each step.

outcomes.why_it_fails: The most likely failure is a stall before real premium volume: carriers retreat on AI risk, there is no loss data to price it and enterprise buyers are slow, so the company never moves from certification to a profitable book. An acquisition by a larger insurer or MGA is the common soft landing.

killers.risk: No carrier capacity or license, so it cannot bind policies
killers.evidence: Armilla relies on Lloyd's coverholder status and others on Beazley paper; carriers are adding AI exclusions rather than taking the risk.
killers.mitigation: Sign an MGA or reinsurer partner before launch, as the SafetyWing experience suggests.

killers.risk: No loss data, so pricing is a guess
killers.evidence: Insurers say AI liability is hard to price due to thin litigation data.
killers.mitigation: Use certification and testing as the underwriting filter and cap limits.

killers.risk: Armilla, Testudo and AIUC already occupy the niche
killers.evidence: Several specialist programs exist, with limits reported up to 25M.
killers.mitigation: Differentiate on self serve and startup focus.

killers.risk: Small team cannot build insurance operations and AI evaluation together
killers.evidence: Team of two with one insurance expert and one engineer.

competition_now.name: Armilla AI
competition_now.what: Standalone AI liability cover with Lloyd's capacity.
competition_now.traction: Limit expanded to 25M per insured, per press.

competition_now.name: Testudo
competition_now.what: Generative AI liability via Lloyd's wholesale.

technical_complexity.rationale: The software to evaluate agents and issue certificates is buildable, but the hard parts are regulatory approval, carrier capacity and actuarial pricing without loss history. A small team can build the evaluation product but not the insurance balance sheet.

takeover_risk.rationale: Specialists already exist, and big carriers could launch AI cover once exclusions create demand. Insurers have the balance sheet and distribution, so a startup depends on a partner carrier that could also build its own.

evidence.claim: Carriers are adding AI exclusions to cyber, E&O and general liability, creating a coverage gap.
Specialist AI liability programs exist and are expanding limits.

roadmap.goal: Secure a carrier or MGA partner and a design customer.

roadmap.proof: 2M gross written premium with controlled losses

roadmap.goal: Become a standalone carrier or leading MGA.

pros.point: Founder with proven insurance product growth
pros.evidence: Grew a product from 5M to 60M revenue at SafetyWing per the YC text.

strengths: Short, friendly, easy to say and hints at claims
weaknesses: Spelling with k and ee reads consumer and may seem less serious to enterprise buyers
brand.rationale: Invented names are common and show no outcome penalty in the name tables. The playful spelling hints at claims but may undercut trust for enterprise risk buyers, a minor effect.

narrative.headline: Hot, real coverage gap with a strong insurance operator, but capacity and loss data decide whether it grows beyond a first round.
narrative.general_summary: Klaimee offers insurance and certification for AI agents. The need is real because carriers are excluding AI claims, and the founder has proven insurance product experience. But armilla-ai, a YC predecessor, already sells this and raised only a seed, and insurance startups need carrier capacity and licenses that take time. A seed is somewhat likelier than not, Series A is about one in four, and the path usually runs through an MGA model before any carrier. Wide uncertainty applies because this is a blind forecast from a short listing, the cohort data is thin, and the seed step is defined as a round above 500K within roughly a year of batch start.

assumptions: Blind test: only the YC listing text was used for the company itself.
Seed means more than 500K within about 12 months of batch start; cohort anchors are for any seed ever.
Recent batches are right censored in the base rates.
Web results dated after the batch start were ignored.
